title: Ghost writing
explanation: A faint 'TOP SECRET' overlay changes thousands of pixels by a few shades, enough to find if you look closely.
simple: It's like writing on a window with a nearly dry marker: it's there, but you have to tilt your head to see it.

title: The hidden picture
explanation: Every pixel's last bit was replaced with a black-and-white picture. Your eyes can't see a change of 1 out of 256, but the bit-0 plane shows it at once.
simple: Imagine changing every price in a shop by one cent. Nobody notices, but if you only look at the cents, a picture appears.

title: Message in the attic
explanation: A text message was written into the last bits row by row from the top, so the top strip of the bit-0 plane looks different from the rest.
simple: Like writing a note in tiny letters along the top edge of a page: hard to see, but easy to find once you know to look at the top.

title: Scattered secrets
explanation: The same message, scattered randomly with a secret key and written by adding or subtracting 1. Without the key, the bit-0 plane looks like normal noise.
simple: Now the letters are sprinkled all over the page, and only someone with the secret key knows which spots to read.
hidden: Meet me at the library at 3pm. Bring the blue notebook. The password is OWL-42. Meet me at the library at 3pm. Bring the...

title: Invisible signature
explanation: A watermark was mixed into the image's frequency bands, the way some AI image tools tag their outputs. It survives saving and is invisible to the eye.
simple: Like a faint pattern woven into fabric: you can't see it, but the right scanner can still read it after the photo is saved again.

title: JPEG smuggler
explanation: JPEGs store 8x8 blocks of frequencies, not pixels. JSteg hides bits in those numbers, which leaves a tell-tale pattern in their histogram.
simple: A JPEG is a recipe for each small square of the photo. JSteg changes the recipe's numbers slightly instead of the pixels.

title: Shrinking numbers
explanation: nsF5 only ever shrinks coefficients toward zero and uses clever coding to make fewer changes, so JSteg's histogram tell disappears.
simple: The same recipe trick, but it only ever makes numbers a little smaller and changes as few as it can, so there are fewer clues.

title: Hide in the grass
explanation: Content-adaptive: each change has a cost, and changes go where the image is already busy. The cost map shows where hiding is cheap.
simple: Like whispering in a noisy room: the changes go where the photo is already busy, so nobody notices them.

title: Master of disguise
explanation: J-UNIWARD measures cost with wavelet filters, so changes land almost only in textured regions where detectors struggle.
simple: An even smarter whisperer: it checks every edge in every direction and only hides where nothing would look out of place.

title: Needle in a haystack
explanation: Very few changes, all in the busiest textures. This is near the limit of what modern steganalysis tools can detect, let alone human eyes.
simple: The same expert hider with a tiny message. Fewer changes means almost nothing to find, even for computers.
